canonical_statement: The chapter reviews unfractionated heparin mechanism of action, pharmacokinetics, anticoagulant effects, laboratory monitoring, clinical use, safety, and emerging low-molecular-weight heparins.
Intravenous heparin has an immediate anticoagulant onset and is used when a rapid anticoagulant effect is required.

Heparin is not absorbed orally and therefore requires parenteral administration; intravenous and subcutaneous routes are preferred and intramuscular injection should be avoided because of hematoma risk.
The review reports that intermittent intravenous heparin injection is associated with more bleeding than continuous intravenous infusion, making continuous infusion the preferred intravenous method.

The review reports comparable efficacy and safety for adequate-dose continuous intravenous and subcutaneous heparin, while emphasizing that subcutaneous loading must account for reduced bioavailability.
Heparin anticoagulant activity is mediated largely by binding of a unique high-affinity pentasaccharide sequence to antithrombin III, accelerating inhibition of thrombin, factor Xa, and factor IXa.

canonical_statement: Heparin binding to plasma proteins contributes to reduced recovery at low concentrations, variable anticoagulant response to fixed doses, and laboratory heparin resistance.
Heparin clearance combines a rapid saturable pathway involving endothelial cells and macrophages with a slower nonsaturable pathway described as largely renal.

Heparin exhibits dose-dependent nonlinear pharmacokinetics: the reported apparent biologic half-life rises from about 30 minutes after 25 U/kg IV to 60 minutes after 100 U/kg IV and 150 minutes after 400 U/kg IV.
Subcutaneous heparin has reduced plasma recovery at low and moderate doses, whereas recovery is reported as almost complete at therapeutic doses above 35,000 U per 24 hours.

In a cited venous-thrombosis study, therapeutic heparin levels and APTT ratios at 24 hours were reported in 37% of patients receiving 15,000 U subcutaneous heparin every 12 hours versus 71% receiving 30,000 U per 24 hours by continuous IV infusion; both regimens used a 5,000 U IV bolus.

canonical_statement: Table 2 classifies bleeding as a common heparin side effect; thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopenia with thrombosis, and osteoporosis as uncommon; and anaphylactic reactions, skin necrosis, local urticaria, and hypoaldosteronism as rare.

A descriptive series cited by the review reported clinical osteoporosis in 6 of 10 patients receiving 15,000 to 20,000 U of heparin daily for more than six months, versus none of 107 patients receiving lower doses.

A 40-patient randomized antenatal prophylaxis trial cited by the review reported clinical osteoporosis in 1 of 20 women assigned to heparin 10,000 U twice daily; the reported 95% confidence interval around the 5% incidence was 0.13% to 24.87%, and no control patient developed the complication.

A pregnancy cohort cited by the review reported radiographic osteopenia in 12 of 70 heparin-treated women (17%) versus none of 30 controls; two women in the high-dose prophylaxis subgroup developed symptomatic postpartum spinal fractures.

The review concludes that clinically important osteoporosis is unlikely with short-term heparin therapy of 14 days or less and also unlikely with about three months of approximately 20,000 U per 24 hours, while most reported cases occurred with at least 20,000 U daily for more than six months.
The review advises considering patients receiving high heparin doses for more than five months to be at significant risk of osteoporosis.
The review reports heparin-associated thrombocytopenia as rare at low prophylactic doses (less than 1%) but also describes cases after heparin catheter flushes.
A pooled analysis of randomized studies cited by the review reported thrombocytopenia in 15.6% of 173 patients receiving bovine-lung heparin versus 5.8% of 223 receiving porcine-gut heparin.

Heparin-associated thrombocytopenia is reported to begin most often 3 to 15 days after starting heparin, with a median near 10 days, but can occur within hours after prior heparin exposure; platelet counts usually return to baseline within about four days after stopping heparin.
The review reports an estimated 0.4% incidence of heparin-induced arterial thrombosis (4 of 1,080) among patients receiving therapeutic porcine-gut heparin.
The review recommends daily platelet counts during heparin therapy and stopping heparin if the platelet count falls progressively or precipitously below 100,000 per microliter.

A washed-platelet serotonin-release test using patient serum and low versus very high heparin concentrations is described as both sensitive and specific for suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
Table 3 describes ancrod as an alternative antithrombotic regimen with an initial dose of 2 U/kg IV over 6 hours followed by fibrinogen-guided subcutaneous or continuous-IV maintenance dosing.

canonical_statement: The review describes selective hypoaldosteronism with hyperkalemia as a rare but probably real heparin adverse effect, supported by three case reports including reversibility after heparin withdrawal in two cases.

Low-molecular-weight heparins are heparin fragments produced by chemical or enzymatic depolymerization, with molecular weights of roughly 1,000 to 10,000 and mean molecular weights around 4,000 to 5,000.

Because only longer LMWH chains can form the antithrombin-heparin-thrombin ternary complex, commercial LMWHs retain proportionally more anti-factor-Xa than anti-factor-IIa activity; reported anti-Xa:anti-IIa ratios range about 4:1 to 2:1 versus approximately 1:1 for standard heparin.

LMWHs bind less to many heparin-binding proteins and endothelial cells, contributing to high subcutaneous bioavailability, more predictable dose response, and plasma half-lives reported as approximately twofold to fourfold longer than standard heparin.
LMWHs are described as being cleared principally by the renal route, with biologic half-life prolonged in renal failure.
Across cited animal thrombosis models, LMWHs are summarized as slightly less effective than standard heparin on a gravimetric basis but as producing much less bleeding in standardized-injury models.

canonical_statement: The review states that longer half-life and more predictable response to weight-adjusted doses permit LMWH administration once daily without routine laboratory monitoring in the studied contexts.

For general surgical patients, the review summarizes LMWH prophylaxis once daily as approximately 30% more effective than standard heparin 5,000 U subcutaneously twice or three times daily for preventing venous thrombosis, without a reported bleeding difference.

In major hip or knee surgery, the review reports about a 70% reduction in thrombosis with LMWH compared with control without increased bleeding, and summarizes direct comparisons as favoring LMWH over several prophylactic alternatives.
In stroke and other high-risk medical patients, the review reports relative reductions in venous thrombosis of roughly 60% to 90% with LMWH without increased clinically important bleeding.
In cited comparisons of LMWH with standard heparin in paralytic stroke and spinal-cord injury, the review reports greater than 70% reductions in thrombosis among patients randomized to LMWH.
The review reports that LMWHs do not cross the placental barrier and notes only descriptive evidence suggesting safety and efficacy during pregnancy.

The review states that an apparently lower incidence of thrombocytopenia with LMWH compared with heparin had not been confirmed in a properly designed clinical study and notes LMWH cross-reactivity with plasma from patients with recent heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

For treatment of venous thrombosis, fixed-dose subcutaneous LMWH is summarized as as effective or more effective than dose-adjusted continuous-infusion heparin by venographic outcomes, with recurrent-event studies showing a strong trend toward greater efficacy and safety.

The authors suggest that the LMWH treatment findings raise the possibility of home treatment for selected patients with venous thrombosis, while explicitly stating that more research is required on unresolved LMWH questions.
